title: The Zen Mirror of Tokeiji
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: The talk's main teaching is that by looking into mirrors - both literal and metaphorical - we can gain insight into our true nature and find freedom from attachment to our physical appearance and identity. This practice allows us to see beyond the surface level of our thoughts, feelings, and body, revealing our inner selves and the interconnectedness of all things. By embracing this awareness, we can transcend our limitations and discover a deeper sense of self that is not bound by ego or material possessions.
topics: Ruth Ozeki's "The Face: A Time Code"

sentences.text: Good morning again, everybody.
I hope everybody's all right as we sit this last full day of sesshin.
This morning I have another case for you from the Hidden Lamp.
It's called the Zen Mirror of Tokaiji.
This is a story from 13th century Japan.
*The convent of Tokaiji had a great mirror.
The founding abbess Kakazon Shido would meditate before this mirror in order to see into her own true nature.
Later generations of nuns would practice zazen in front of the mirror, concentrating on the question, "Where is a single feeling, a single thought, in the mirror image at which I gaze?"
Each abbess of Tokaiji wrote a verse in response to the mirror practice.
The following verse was composed by the fifth abbess, Princess Yodo.*
And here's the verse.
*Heart unclouded, heart clouded, standing or falling, it's still the same body.*
When Florence and Sue compiled the stories from the Hidden Lamp, they looked far and wide to find them.
Actually, there are quite a number of stories about women in the Buddhist tradition.
But mostly the ones we know and the ones that are most readily available are about men.
So Florence and Sue did a lot of research.
A tremendous amount of work went into this book on a lot of levels.
One of the texts that they uncovered was the Shonan Kato Roku, the Shonan Koan record, which was a Kamakura period collection of Japanese Zen koans.
The Kamakura period was a little bit after Dogen's time.
Dogen, as you know, was one of the really early people to practice Zen in Japan.
He went to China and brought back from China the understanding of his teacher Ru Jing, as well as some texts.
But as soon as he came to Japan, he was speaking about these texts in his own way in Japanese for Japanese practitioners.
But at that same time and later after that, a lot of Chinese teachers came to Japan.

I guess it's quite analogous to the way it is now, where especially some years ago, you had a lot of teachers from Tibet, teachers from Japan, teachers from Korea, some teachers from China, who were here in the West, bringing what they felt was the authentically acculturated Buddhism of their cultures to us.
And mostly they thought they needed to bring it in their cultural context because our culture didn't include it.
The same thing went on in those early days in Japan, where there were a lot of Chinese teachers.
Many of them didn't speak Japanese, so they were speaking about Chinese koans in Chinese.
And just like now, people complain: why do we have to chant all this in Japanese?
This is so Japanese, can't we make it American?
People complain.
Same thing there.
They said, can't we make this Chinese thing Japanese?
So they wanted to have Japanese koans, and they began creating collections of Japanese koans.
These exist, and some of them have been translated.
A recent one just came out, but mostly we study the classical Chinese koans.

I think that in the American lineages that practice the koan tradition as it was shaped by Hakuen Zenji in Japan in the 18th century, while the koans are all Chinese, they're supplemented with so-called checking koans, which are mostly from the Japanese tradition.
Anyway, this text, the Shonan Kato Roku, is one such Japanese koan text.
And probably one reason why this particular text is a little obscure, and a lot of American practitioners wouldn't be attracted to it, is that the Kamakura period was the samurai period.
So the Zen in those days was focused on warrior practice.
A lot of the samurai warlords were patrons of the Zen tradition.
I think we're not so interested, right, in practicing Zen so that we can kill people without blinking an eye.
I don't think that's what we're trying to do here.
But it just goes to show you how, for better and worse, how flexible the Zen tradition is, how flexible any religious tradition is.
It could be this, it could be that.
Same teaching, same practice.
You can emphasize it in very different ways, right?
A lot of the stories in the Shonan Kato Roku include legends and tales about the samurai and different events in Japanese history that Japanese people would be familiar with.
The stories include lots of wonder-working Zen masters.
There's one guy who shouts, and people fall down dead after he shouts.
Amazing.
Also, the collection happens to include quite a number of stories of tough women who held their own during this period.
And this is a story from that collection.
Although, as we heard, it doesn't particularly have anything to do with samurai or warriors.
If you're interested in this text, it was translated in 1985 by Trevor Leggett under the title *Samurai Zen: The Warrior Koans*.
You can find a PDF of it and download it.
It's kind of interesting, actually.
Anyway, in the Shonan Kato Roku there's a lot of background to the main story, and the background has lots of Japanese historical stuff in it.
But the basic story about the mirror is worth telling, I think.
So how did it come to be that there's a mirror?
It seems odd, right?
I don't think any of us has ever walked into a zendo that has a big mirror in it, right?
So how come there's a mirror in this great zendo at Tokaiji?
You might think, well, it's nuns, so they like to look at themselves in the mirror.
But no, men also like to look at themselves in the mirror.
That's not why there's a mirror in Tokaiji.
Sorry about my scratchy throat today.

So long, long ago, in the shadowy, dreamy era of magical and medieval Japan, there was a nun who had a dream of a great mirror floating in the waves off Yue Beach, which I guess was a famous place in Japan.
So she dreamed of a mirror.
It would be something to see, a mirror floating in the ocean, right, reflecting all the waves of the ocean.
She dreamed of this mirror, a very vivid dream, and the mirror was talking.
The mirror said to her in the dream, "I am the voice of the great shrine at Yue, and the entire future is reflected in me.
And there is a war coming, and the army must be mobilized."

She had this dream, and she told people about it, and the word got to the local warlord, who sent emissaries to the great shrine at Yue Beach, and they prayed for the peace of the land, while of course also mobilizing the troops, just in case.
And wouldn't you know it, there was a war.
Because this warlord had been forewarned by the nun's dream, and had prepared for the war, he was victorious.
In commemoration of his great victory, he had a mirror made six foot in circumference, following exactly the description of the great spirit mirror in the nun's dream.
And he had this mirror installed in the great shrine at Yue.

But since Japanese history, like all history, is basically the story of disasters, and catastrophes, and overthrowings of regimes, and destruction, over and over and over again, eventually the great shrine at Yue was destroyed.
The mirror was removed and stolen, removed and stolen again and again and again, until it eventually ended up in the great mirror hall, the great mirror hall of Tokaiji Monastery.
What in the world is a great mirror hall?
I never knew about any monasteries having great mirror halls.
I don't know exactly, but I do know that in Yogachara Buddhist thought, which is part of our tradition too, we have the idea of the great mirror awareness.
The great mirror awareness, in a word, is the transformation of the alaya vijnana, which occurs when the mind turns in awakening, so that there's no gap in reality.
There's no distortion.
Everything is reflected just as it is in a perfect mirror.
Everything is perfect and beautiful in great mirror awareness.
There's also, based on that teaching, the famous poem we all know of the sixth ancestor about a mirror.
*The body is a mirror stand.
The mind is a mirror.
We should carefully wipe it clean with our practice.*
But no, the sixth ancestor writes in his poem, there is no stand, there is no mirror, so what is there to wipe clean?

And also, in Chinese Buddhist history, in the Avatamsaka school, there's the famous hall of mirrors of Fatsang, who, wanting to show the truth of how in each and every atom everywhere there is a Buddha, made a room of mirrors.
Floor, ceiling, walls, only mirrors.
In the middle of this room he placed a table, and on the table he put a golden Buddha image, so that when you walked into the room, you saw an infinite regress of Buddhas everywhere you looked.
Anyway, who knows, maybe in medieval Japan, in some places they had great mirror halls that were installed to illustrate these teachings, I don't know.
But in any case, during this period in Japan, Zen was introduced and became very quickly the dominant school.
So the great mirror hall at Tokaiji monastery was eventually converted into a zendo.
And although it's very unusual, the nuns decided to keep this famous historical and mythical mirror in the zendo.
So the abbesses of this nunnery, for many generations, used this mirror, and [unclear: "there's how Zen practiced"], as the story describes.
A number of them wrote poems about the mirror practice, and these poems became the secret koan treasure house of this particular nunnery.
In the Shonan Kato Roku, eight poems are included, but in their version of the story, Florence and Sue quoted just one of the poems.
So I'll just quickly give you a few of the others that they didn't include.
This is the poem of the founder, the nun Shido.
*If the mind does not rest on anything, there's no clouding, and talk of polishing is but a fancy.*
The poem of the second teacher, the nun Runkai:
*Various reflections, yet its surface is unscarred.
From the very beginning, unclouded, the pure mirror.*
The poem that Florence and Sue quote in their book is by the fifth abbess:
*Heart unclouded, heart clouded, standing or falling.
It is still the same body.*
This one is probably the best poem for us.
I see why Florence and Sue, who come from the heart of our tradition, would have chosen it.
It reminds us of Dogen, it reminds us of Suzuki Roshi, who were appreciative of the depth of our ordinary up and down human life.
Really, it seems to us like a kind of strange idea to sit zazen facing a mirror and to use, in effect, the image of one's own body as a koan.
But what a great koan, right?
What is this body?
We have a very possessive concept of the body.
We think the body is us, this is my body, this is what I look like.
And then we have so many unexamined feelings and associations and almost ungraspable, vague musings about this body.
But really, what is this body?
It is quite strange, really.
And as the nuns ask in their koan practice, what about all the thoughts and feelings that pass through?
Where are they?
How real are they?
This reminds me of a little book by Ruth Ozeki, who many of you know well, our dear Ruth, a priest in our Dharma family, and of course a world-class novelist.
I'm sure many of you read her novel *A Tale for the Time Being*.
And you're in luck, because she just finished another one.
It's about to come out, I think, in the fall.
It's also very, very good.
I've read it.
Anyway, this is not one of her novels.
This is a little book that I think she was asked to write for a series.
This book is called *The Face: A Time Code*.
The book is about an experiment that Ruth conducted of looking in a mirror at her face for three hours straight and writing about what she experienced as she did that.
She actually goes minute by minute, but then there's many asides where she reflects on what she's feeling.
It's all about, what is our face?
Face is a miracle.
You can see so much in the face, the expressions.
Sometimes you see an expression on the face, and there's so much to it.
You can't even say what that is, what that's expressing.
But there's so much there, the eyes, different ways the face is moving.
So Ruth really went through her whole life in these three hours of looking at her face.
I won't read much of it, but just to give you an idea, I'll read a little bit of what she writes here.
The cover of the book is kind of nice because it has that, I don't know what you call it, but there's an app that you can make a cartoon of your face.
It still looks like you, but it's kind of like a cartoon.
Well, that is a cartoon of Ruth's face on the cover, and it's very, very haunting.
It looks like Ruth, but of course, it doesn't look like Ruth.
Anyway, here's a time code.
*00 colon 00 colon 00.
I put the mirror on the altar where the Buddha used to be.
Laptop just below it.
Fussing now with the seating, arranging the cushions.
How close should I be?
And how much proximity can I tolerate?
How's the lighting?
Flattering?
Unflattering?
Does it matter?
Should I change into a turtleneck to hide the lines on my neck?
Hide them from who?
Is the neck even part of the face?
And do I need to wash my hair?
Do I need reading glasses, or can I type without them?
Can I see without them?*
*No.
No glasses.
No need to look at the computer screen.
Just facing me.
Facing off in the mirror.
Now it's four minutes and 14 seconds later.
Okay.
Ready.
No, wait.
There's dust on the mirror.
Must clean it.
Do I have vinegar?
Yes, under the sink.
Now it's seven minutes and 26 seconds.
Mirror's spotless.
Eight minutes and 56 seconds.
How do I start?
Ten minutes and 12 seconds.*
*Staring at my face.
I'm aware that I want to touch it.
Touch the scar on my forehead.
The pimple on my chin.
Rub my nose.
My eyes.
Scratch my cheek.
I'm aware that everything looks wrong.
My face, my hair, my collar.
And I want to fix things.
I run my fingers through my hair, pulling it back from my face.
It falls forward again like a curtain.
It's trying to shield me from myself.
Nice.
I spent much of my life hiding behind this curtain of hair.
Thirteen minutes and two seconds.
When I look myself in the eye, it's hard to look away.*
*Eyes define a face.
If we were not such visual creatures, if we received our sensory input some other way, maybe we would not need faces.
Trees don't have faces.
Jellyfish don't need faces.
Daisies do.
And they don't have eyes.
So perhaps I'm wrong about this.*
*Fourteen minutes and 37 seconds.
Still watching the eyes.
Sad.
Serious.
Brown.
Slanting downward.
The angle of the slope seems more pronounced, more acute than I'd realized.
Have my eyes changed?
My eyelids are heavier.
The folds of skin almost meet the lashes.
The right eye and the left eye are very different.
The left eye looks slightly more Asiatic.
The right epicanthic fold is more pronounced, making that eye look more Caucasian.
I used to notice this when I put on eyeliner.
But here's something I've never noticed before, or at least never admitted.
I have a preference.*
*It's subtle.
But I've always preferred my right eye to my left.
I've preferred my Caucasian eye to my Asian eye.
Strange.
When the nuns of Tokeiji looked into the mirror, they saw nuns with shaved heads dressed in dark robes and wrapped in okesas.*
This is one aspect of sesshin that we don't usually talk about too much.
One of the practices in sesshin is wearing clothes.
Many of us, it's a particular characteristic somehow of everyday Zen sanghas, that many, many of us, not all of us by any means, but many of us wear Buddha's robe, rakusu or okesa.
Some of us wear traditional koromo under the okesa.
So we also look like the nuns of Tokeiji dressed in Buddhist clothing.
As we say in the ceremony when you receive your Buddhist robe, this will be your clothing from now on, in this lifetime and in lives to come.
I know that for me, wearing clothes is a big part of sesshin.
When I'm in sesshin, I wear my robes pretty much all day long.
And I feel my life differently.
My body is a different body.
I walk differently.
I move differently.

And among the great pleasures that we have heard about, that we're missing at Samish when we're there together in person, is the pleasure of seeing each other slowly moving across the big expanse of lawn in our dark clothing, in our robes, moving like Buddhas, dignified and mindful.
And we make ever-changing human patterns in space, which are every bit as wondrous as the swallows and the sunsets.
Wearing clothes is a practice.
It conditions who we are.
In different historical periods of time, people wore different kinds of clothing because they were different kinds of people.
So wearing clothing is a practice always.
It conditions who we are, how we feel about ourselves and our lives.
When we look in a mirror or when we see our reflection in the glass doors of the zendo, the basketball court church zendo in Samish, when we approach that door, we see a living Buddha.
As I said the other day, and as probably all of you know, because most of you know The Hidden Lamp, each one of the stories has a commentary written by a different contemporary teacher.
And this one is by a Zen teacher that I really admire, and I'm lucky to have her for a friend: Zenju Earthlyn Manuel, who is really a very unusual Zen teacher.
Very poetic.
She's a beautiful writer.
So I'm going to read you what she says in response to this story.
*Where is a single feeling, a single thought in the mirror image at which I gaze?
When we ask this question, we immediately enter the purpose of our lives, which is to look upon our lives and discover who we are as living beings.
We enter a dark abyss in which we encounter our heart, mind, and body.
On the journey of discovery we fall through the sky.
At times the sky is clouded, at other times unclouded.
On the earth we plant our feet, and yet we stumble.
What are the clouds, and what takes them away?
What makes us stand or fall?
Looking into the mirror may seem easy, but being honest with what we see is difficult.
A few days before my 59th birthday, I looked into the mirror to see if I looked old.
And I asked, am I old?
What is old?
I did this exercise for five minutes a day, for seven days.*
A little bit like what Ruth did, right?
*On the first day I didn't see anything, because I was afraid of seeing an old lady.
My eyes constantly turned away.
On the second day I spent time plucking the hairs from my chin.
I could see clearly the white hairs against my dark skin.
They provided a nice distraction.
On the third day I thought I should grow my hair longer, so that the thinning parts would disappear.
I remember my mother's hair thinning in the same places when she was my age.
Still, I didn't want to see my mother in me, nor see an old lady in myself.
On the fourth day as I looked in the mirror I wondered, what does an old lady look like?
So I spent much of my day examining women as I walked in the world, deciding who looked old and who didn't.
On the fifth day I decided I must be old, because my neck skin was beginning to sag like I had seen in the so-called old women in the day before.*
Yes, Ruth mentions the neck too.
I guess that's all saying, the neck is the first thing to go.
They say that.
It's true.
*On the sixth day I cried in front of the mirror, because I felt I had no control over my stumbling into old age, and I felt my death was closer than ever before.
On the seventh day I saw fear in the tightness of my lips, confusion in the brow.
I thought, what a tough journey life is.
Then I looked deeper, without any idea in my head, just the question, what is old?
And I saw a courageous woman, willing at least to look at herself.
There are many mirrors.*
*A physical mirror can reveal expressions on our faces.
The mirror of Zazen allows us to look into the heart and body mirror.
When I look at the mirror, I see a black face.
In the past I have responded to being black with painful emotions.
However, through Zazen, when I see my black face, I am awake to the suffering that arises.
I see the old pain rising in the moment of looking in the mirror.
I wait for my response to pass, as it is guaranteed to do.
And in that passing, I see more of who I am, and not so much how I appear.*
*When we face the mirror of Zazen, our minds tend to face ourselves as objects.
First, our skin color, age, gender, sexual orientation, all the ways we are embedded and move in the world.
We begin to unfold stories about I.
If we are willing to look long enough in the mirror of Zazen, past seeing ourselves as objects, we have the potential to see that we are nature itself.
We are born and will die, just like the trees, flowers, and animals will do.
And sometimes in Zazen, we see that the mirror is clean, clear, no clouds, no dust.*
*The human condition is set aside.
I am not old, middle-aged, or young.
I am fulfilled in my own spirit.
And in this recognition, I feel the connection to my ancestors, to those who came before me, and to a life larger than my own.
I am returned to an open field in which there are many possibilities.
This open field is my original home, where there is no blackness and no old age, as Princess Yodo wrote, heart unclouded, heart clouded, standing or falling, it's still the same body.*
*I say, in the silence of my open field, face clear or face colorful, dancing or sitting, it is still the same body.*
And Sue and Florence, at the end of all these commentaries, add their own koan.
And here's their koan.
*What do you see when you look in the mirror?
Are you there?*
So I close my talk this morning with just one other short paragraph, beautiful paragraph, from Zenju Earthlyn.
This is from her book that just came out recently, called The Deepest Peace.
She lived a long time in Oakland, and now she lives in New Mexico, I think in Santa Fe, maybe.
And she spends a lot of time alone in the desert.
This is just a short passage from that book.
By the way, she has the most glorious smile when she smiles.
She's very quiet, and when she smiles, her whole face lights up, Earthlyn says.
Quite joyful to see her.
*In the quiet morning, there are words to be written.
I must catch them as they fly about my house.
First, the past, the ancient story, lands.
The breath takes over to allow the body to write.
Next, the silence takes the pen.
The silence is not talking or writing, it's arising from the quiet.
What the silence is saying is revealed in my writing.
How do I know what is to be written?
How do I translate a voice coming through silence?
I have no doubt.
I have heard the words over and over again throughout my life.
You have probably heard the same message of wisdom.
And yet, the words must be repeated, century after century.
All wisdom is from the Earth.
I connect to the Earth by observing it, communing with it as it speaks.
First, it may be the mind shattering.
Next, the interpretation of the shattering.
Then the confusion.
Then the not knowing.
Next, silence.
And more silence.
And then finally, a silence that I could have never imagined.
We must find a way to the voice of life's mysteries.
If not through silence, then through whatever means called to us.*
So I thank you all again for listening to my talk.
Some of you have listened to so many of my talks over so many years that you probably know what I'm going to say before I even say it.
You don't even need to listen anymore.
So thank you not only for listening today, but all the days.
And I hope that you will all have a peaceful, silent day for the rest of today.
*May our intention equally extend to every being and place with the true merit of Buddha's way.
Beings are numberless.
I vow to save them.
Illusions are inexhaustible.
I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless.
I vow to enter them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable.
I vow to become it.*
